summary: British biotech firm Colorifix has launched Sunlit Clay, a warm earthy shade for wool. The dye is produced using engineered bacteria, offering a lower‑impact alternative to petrochemical dyes. The com...
content: British biotech firm Colorifix has launched Sunlit Clay, a warm earthy shade for wool. The dye is produced using engineered bacteria, offering a lower‑impact alternative to petrochemical dyes. The company announced the new shade on September 29, saying Sunlit Clay is available in both yarn and fabric and is produced using its proprietary biological dyeing technology. Courtesy: Collected The color was inspired by bacteria found in soil and deep-sea sediments, with the company showcasing a 100% wool swatch. Based at Norwich Research Park, Colorifix was co-founded by University of Cambridge scientist Jim Ajioka and Chief Executive Orr Yarkoni. The company began in 2013 with research into sensors for detecting heavy metals in drinking water before turning its attention to textile dyeing after witnessing the environmental impact of conventional dyeing in Nepal and Bangladesh. Colorifix says it has developed an entirely biological process to produce, deposit and fix pigments on textiles. The technology starts with DNA instructions for a natural pigment, sourced from public databases, which are inserted into bacteria or yeast. The engineered microorganisms are grown in fermenters using agricultural by-products. The process is similar to brewing, with the resulting fermentation material pumped into conventional dyeing machines together with yarn, fabric or garments. Heat breaks open the microbial cells and releases the pigment, allowing it to bond with the textile fiber. The remaining cells are subsequently washed away. The company says its technology can be used on cotton, wool, silk, polyester, nylon and lyocell and can operate with existing textile mill infrastructure. content: EMIGSVILLE, PA — September 30, 2026 — Herculite Products Inc., an innovator in High Performance and Custom Fabrics with recognized brands such as Coastline Plus and Patio 500, is pleased to announce that Humberto Medrano has been hired as Regional Sales Manager covering the Southwest to develop and grow relationships with End Product Manufacturers and related sales personnel for all Awning and Marine brands and to promote awareness, loyalty, and consumption of our industry-leading awning fabric brands through our distribution partners. Humberto Medrano Humberto holds a Bachelor of Science in Electronic Engineering from DeVry University. He has more than 40 years of international and domestic sales and account management experience, including over 20 in the textile industry. He currently lives in Azusa, California, is a dad to four amazing grown children, and a grandfather to two beautiful little girls. Humberto enjoys baseball and has played and coached in his spare time; one of his children played at the college level, and the other played in the Mexican professional league. At Herculite, we are committed to delivering the highest level of service, support, and innovation in the industry. We are confident that Humberto’s experience, communication skills, and customer-focused approach will make him a valuable addition to our team and enable him to contribute meaningfully to our mission. title: EU regulations and brand commitments are creating a stronger market for recycled fiber
summary: Recycled fiber is moving beyond isolated sustainability projects. Major fashion brands are signing long-term purchase agreements with recycling companies before many recycling plants reach full comm...
content: Recycled fiber is moving beyond isolated sustainability projects. Major fashion brands are signing long-term purchase agreements with recycling companies before many recycling plants reach full commercial scale. Figure: Next-generation recycled fiber currently costs 30% to 80% more than virgin fossil polyester or bottle-derived rPET. Primark signed a multi-year offtake agreement with Circ to use recycled polyester made from textile waste starting in 2029. The deal supports Circ’s planned industrial facility in Saint-Avold, France. Circ gains a committed customer for planned production, while Primark secures access to future recycled polyester supply. This process marks the start of a new supply chain. A recycler develops technology, and a brand commits to buying output. An industrial producer converts output into fiber, allowing manufacturers to bring the material into mainstream production. Why offtake agreements matter Textile recycling requires collecting waste, sorting materials, removing contaminants, and converting waste into usable polymer or fiber. Recycling companies need industrial buyers to process material consistently. Without confirmed buyers, recyclers struggle to raise capital for large factories. Without a reliable fiber supply, brands cannot meet material targets. Long-term offtake agreements provide recyclers with visible future revenue. H&M Group signed a seven-year offtake agreement with Syre valued at $600 million to cover a large share of its recycled polyester needs. Syre also built relationships with Gap, Target, and Houdini. These deals brought its secured brand offtakes close to $900 million. Inditex signed a three-year deal worth over €70 million to purchase cycora recycled polyester from Ambercycle. summary: SACRAMENTO, CA— October 6, 2026 — The Nature Conservancy (TNC) has launched the Microfiber Action Alliance (MAA), a new multi-stakeholder initiative to combat microfiber pollution by accelerating the adoption and scaling of effective, evidence-based solutions. content: SACRAMENTO, CA— October 6, 2026 — The Nature Conservancy (TNC) has launched the Microfiber Action Alliance (MAA), a new multi-stakeholder initiative to combat microfiber pollution by accelerating the adoption and scaling of effective, evidence-based solutions. Convened by TNC, the founding cohort includes Nike, Patagonia, Under Armour, lululemon, Cotopaxi and REI Co-op, among other leading brands. Microfibers are small particles that shed from both synthetic and natural textiles. Alongside use and wear, the production of clothing and textiles is a significant contributor to microfiber pollution globally, with some estimates indicating that microfibers account for over 30% of ocean microplastics. While synthetic microfibers are among the most common forms of microplastic pollution found in nature, even natural fibers, such as cotton and wool, contribute to microfiber pollution if they have been treated with dye, softeners or finishes. Once in the environment, microfibers are extremely difficult to remove because they are so small and easily dispersed, underscoring the importance of prevention. Fortunately, a range of effective solutions exist. Complementing the work of The Microfibre Consortium, which convenes across the textile industry to develop the science, data and tools needed to reduce fiber fragmentation, TNC will work with participating companies to better understand, refine and advance solutions that can meaningfully reduce microfiber pollution. title: Turkey’s rising demand opens new playbook for RMG exports
summary: Key points Exports to Turkey doubled YoY to $210.54M in Q1 FY2026‑27 Opportunity beyond apparel: MMF, technical textiles, jute, footwear Trade fairs, buyer-seller meetings and B2B engagement can help...
content: Key points Exports to Turkey doubled YoY to $210.54M in Q1 FY2026‑27 Opportunity beyond apparel: MMF, technical textiles, jute, footwear Trade fairs, buyer-seller meetings and B2B engagement can help Bangladeshi exporters Turkey’s labor shift creates supply gap Bangladesh can fill Bangladesh’s sharp export growth in Turkey opens opportunities beyond shipment volumes. Stakeholders urge a targeted strategy to diversify and move toward higher‑value products. Bangladesh exported $210.54 million worth of goods to Turkey in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27, more than double the $105.21 million recorded in the same period a year earlier, according to the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB). Notably, Turkey’s growth supports Bangladesh’s export diversification drive. The bigger opportunity lies in MMF, technical textiles, and other value‑added products beyond traditional apparel. Industry observers say changing labor dynamics in Turkey could create further room for Bangladeshi apparel suppliers. As rising incomes and living standards encourage Turkish workers to move away from labor-intensive garment production, a supply gap is gradually emerging in the domestic market. This could benefit Bangladesh, which has a large production base, competitive pricing and experience in supplying global apparel brands. “Turkey has become a promising market for Bangladesh’s RMG exports,” said Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, Executive President of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) and Managing Director, Fatullah Apparels Ltd. He said Bangladesh could deepen its presence by combining production capacity with product quality, competitive prices and reliable delivery. title: Europe is redrawing its textile investment map, Bangladesh must shift its bet
summary: Europe’s textile industry is quietly changing where capital goes. Investment is moving beyond physical expansion toward circular infrastructure, digital supply chains, low-carbon processing, and advan...
content: Europe’s textile industry is quietly changing where capital goes. Investment is moving beyond physical expansion toward circular infrastructure, digital supply chains, low-carbon processing, and advanced material research. Bangladesh, meanwhile, continues to invest heavily in basic capacity. This widening gap could weaken its Ready-Made Garment (RMG) export position in Europe unless manufacturers shift from volume-led growth to value-led investment. Figure: European Commission estimates that reaching just 10% recycling could save 440,000 metric tons of annual carbon emissions and 8.8 billion cubic meters of water. The clearest signal is Europe’s growing focus on textile waste as a strategic raw material. A Boston Consulting Group and ReHubs study estimates that scaling textile-to-textile recycling to 15% by 2035 will require €8 billion–€11 billion in capital expenditure, plus €5 billion–€6.5 billion in annual operating costs. The European Commission estimates that reaching just 10% recycling could save 440,000 metric tons of annual carbon emissions and 8.8 billion cubic meters of water. Digitalization and clean manufacturing are also attracting capital. EU-backed programs are supporting Industry 4.0 automation, digital tracking and circular design, while Horizon Europe has allocated €450 million for biodegradable polymers and closed-loop synthetic recycling. The Digital Product Passport (DPP) is reinforcing this direction by making product-level data, fiber origin and traceability increasingly central to market access. Recent trade data shows the gap. Bangladesh’s apparel exports to the EU fell 16.43% to €8.64 billion in H1 2026. Volume fell 8.22% and unit prices dropped 8.94% to €13.88 per kilogram. title: Bangladesh’s garments industry at a turning point (Part: 1)
summary: For much of the past several months, the conversation around Bangladesh’s garments industry has been dominated by crisis. Gas shortages are disrupting production, electricity remains uncertain in ma...
content: For much of the past several months, the conversation around Bangladesh’s garments industry has been dominated by crisis. Gas shortages are disrupting production, electricity remains uncertain in many industrial areas, geopolitical tensions are affecting energy and shipping routes, costs are rising and international buyers are becoming increasingly cautious about delivery reliability. These concerns are real, and anyone working closely with the industry knows that they are not simply issues being discussed in boardrooms. They are being felt on factory floors, in production planning meetings and in the financial decisions manufacturers have to make every day. Yet there is another side of the Bangladesh story that deserves equal attention. Beneath the immediate difficulties is an industry that has spent more than three decades building something that is extremely difficult to reproduce elsewhere: a large-scale manufacturing ecosystem supported by experienced workers, established supplier networks, increasingly sophisticated factories and a growing culture of social and environmental responsibility. The question now is not simply whether the industry can survive another difficult period. The more important question is whether Bangladesh can use this period of pressure to build a stronger and more competitive industrial model. Bangladesh’s position in the global apparel market has never really been based on cheap labor alone. Price is important, of course, but an international buyer placing a large order needs much more than a competitive FOB. The buyer needs confidence that a factory can maintain quality across large volumes, manage raw materials, meet technical requirements, comply with social and environmental standards and deliver on time. title: Madagascar apparel sector shifts from cost to resilience
summary: Madagascar is seeking to strengthen its apparel industry by combining its low-cost manufacturing advantage with stronger compliance, value addition, and supply chain resilience. Figure:Madagascar ran...
content: Madagascar is seeking to strengthen its apparel industry by combining its low-cost manufacturing advantage with stronger compliance, value addition, and supply chain resilience. Figure:Madagascar ranked second among sub-Saharan African textile and apparel exporters to the US and first to the EU in 2023. The textile and apparel sector remains a major part of the economy, supporting about 180,000 formal jobs and accounting for roughly 25% of the country’s exports, according to the International Labour Organization. The United States remains an important market. Madagascar ranked second among sub-Saharan African textile and apparel exporters to the US and first to the EU in 2023, according to the US International Trade Administration. The sector also provided more than 400,000 direct and indirect jobs in 2025, reflecting its wider economic impact. But the industry faces a major trade challenge. The end of African Growth and Opportunity Act preferences and changes in US tariffs have increased pressure on export competitiveness. In January 2026, Madagascar’s textile employers warned that about 7,000 direct jobs could be at risk from reduced orders. The response is increasingly focused on diversification and higher value production. An IFC project running through 2028 aims to strengthen the sector’s regulatory environment and diversify export markets. For Madagascar, the next phase is therefore not simply about producing apparel at lower cost. It is about building a more resilient export model based on compliance, productivity, market diversification, and higher-value manufacturing.

title: DroneStop provides passive drone defence
summary: KnitMesh Technologies has showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe in London, highlighting the role of physical protection in layered defence against hostile and unauthorised drones. Executive Chairman Lew Bingham and Security and Defence Business Development Manager Andrew De-Gol represented the UK manufacturer during the two-day event, meeting defence and security professionals, […] The post DroneStop provides passive drone defence appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: KnitMesh Technologies has showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe in London, highlighting the role of physical protection in layered defence against hostile and unauthorised drones. Executive Chairman Lew Bingham and Security and Defence Business Development Manager Andrew De-Gol represented the UK manufacturer during the two-day event, meeting defence and security professionals, existing customers and potential international partners. Developed, manufactured and tested by KnitMesh Technologies in the UK, DroneStop is a high-performance Counter-UAS solution designed to help mitigate risks associated with hostile and unauthorised drones. The system uses lightweight, high-strength stainless steel knitted mesh to provide a passive physical barrier that can operate alongside electronic and procedural countermeasures. It requires no power, jamming or radio frequency interference and can be incorporated into existing security infrastructure for temporary or permanent installations. Executive Chairman Lew Bingham (right) and Security and Defence Business Development Manager Andrew De-Gol at Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe in London. © KnitMesh Technologies Potential applications include military and defence facilities, critical national infrastructure, prisons and other secure environments where physical protection against drones is required. KnitMesh said discussions at the London event demonstrated growing interest in physical barriers as an additional layer within wider Counter-UAS strategies. “It was a very worthwhile few days at the European Counter-UAS Conference in London, with plenty of good conversations, shared experiences and lessons learned from across the defence and security community,” said De-Gol. summary: Bangladesh’s green factory movement is moving beyond buildings and certifications. The next challenge is to make production itself more resource-efficient, less carbon-intensive, and more resilient....
content: Bangladesh’s green factory movement is moving beyond buildings and certifications. The next challenge is to make production itself more resource-efficient, less carbon-intensive, and more resilient. Figure1: Karotoa Green Spinning Mills Ltd, Kaliakair, Gazipur Karotoa Green Spinning Mills Ltd is taking that approach at its new manufacturing complex in Kaliakair, Gazipur. Energy, water, natural resources, and worker well-being have been incorporated directly into the design of the factory. The project is being developed on a 90-acre site with four planned production units and an estimated investment of around Tk 2,400 crore. The completed complex is planned to produce 70,000 kilograms of yarn per day. A key focus of the complex is renewable energy. Karotoa plans to generate 6 MW of solar power through rooftop installations across the factory. Solar panels have already been installed in one unit. For the textile sector of Bangladesh, this approach has growing importance as factories face pressure to reduce dependence on fossil fuels, manage energy costs, and respond to decarbonization expectations from global buyers. According to industry reports, Bangladesh already has one of the strongest green-factory bases in the world, with 290 LEED-certified RMG factories recorded by July 2026. Karotoa is also building water management into its core production model. 6 acres of land have been developed on the premises. Water from the pond will be treated and reused in the factory, while rainwater will be captured, purified, and returned to the water system. This closed-loop approach can reduce pressure on freshwater sources and improve overall resource efficiency. content: FRANKFURT, Germany — September 30, 2026 — At the general meeting of VDMA Textile Machinery held in Hanover at the end of September, Dr Janpeter Horn, Managing Director of A. Herzog Maschinenfabrik, was re-elected as Chairman of the trade association. Regina Brückner, managing partner of Brückner Trockentechnik, and Verena Thies, managing partner of Thies Textilmaschinen, will once again serve as vice-chairs for the next four years. Newly elected Executive Board of VDMA Textile Machinery The general meeting of the VDMA Textile Machinery Association took place in the trade fair city of Hanover, one year ahead of the leading trade fair, ITMA. The event’s theme, “The world is moving forward – where is Europe?”, outlined the industry’s current landscape: increasing competition from Asia, coupled with challenging business conditions in Europe, has led to significant declines in order intake and turnover in recent years. Although the turnover forecast for 2026 had to be revised downwards to -14 per cent (nominal), order intake appears to be stabilising. “The discussions and workshops at our General Assembly clearly demonstrated that our industry is in the midst of profound change. The challenges are considerable, yet we possess the innovative strength, the expertise and the technological leadership to actively shape these changes. Together, we will work to support our customers even more effectively throughout the entire lifecycle of their machinery and equipment, to capitalise on the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, and to strengthen the competitiveness of the European textile machinery industry in the long term. The fans are light weighted and expected to provide more savings that the earlier one. Carbon Fiber – Glass Filled Reinforced Poly-amide Blades. R Devaganeshan, Project Head, Tesco Airtechniques Engineering for Energy Efficiency, Durability and for more Sustainable solution. The global textile industry is entering an era where energy efficiency is no longer an option – it is a competitive necessity. Textile manufacturing is inherently energy-intensive, with continuous operations requiring large amounts of electricity for spinning, weaving, processing, humidification, ventilation and other auxiliary systems. At the same time, manufacturers across the world are facing increasing pressure to control production costs, improve energy efficiency and reduce their environmental footprint. Electricity demand globally continues to grow, while energy markets remain exposed to price volatility and supply-side uncertainties. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global electricity demand to grow by around 3.6% in 2026 and 3.8% in 2027. For energy intensive industries, every unit of electricity saved can directly contribute to improved operating economics and competitiveness. Against this backdrop, Tesco Fans has taken another step forward in fan technology – moving from Polyamide Glass Blades to Carbon Fiber Polyamide Glass Blades. content: With 100% of its ring and open-end spinning machinery now connected to its AI-based data analytics platform, The Mill Mind, Sri Kannapiran Mills is converting machine data into actionable intelligence to improve productivity, quality and operational responsiveness — without investing in new equipment. For years, textile mills have installed sophisticated monitoring systems across spinning and weaving operations. However, the availability of data does not necessarily translate into better decision-making. Mr. Srihari Balakrishnan, Managing Director, Sri Kannapiran Mills, believes the industry has historically collected enormous amounts of machine data without fully exploiting its potential. Mr. Srihari Balakrishnan, Managing Director, Sri Kannapiran Mills “As spinners we all have and had data monitoring equipment. Spindle monitoring, carding monitoring, preparatory monitoring etc. Like most of us we were using it as an ornament, not using the data. Not analysing it, not mining it, not drilling down to first principles,” he says. Sri Kannapiran Mills is now attempting to bridge that gap through The Mill Mind, its AI-based data analytics platform. 100% Spinning Capacity Under AI-Based Monitoring The company has now connected its ring and open-end spinning machines across all four spinning locations to The Mill Mind. Data from the machines flows continuously into the platform, where it is analysed for consistency and deviations. Depending on the process, alerts are generated either immediately or at the end of a shift or day, allowing manufacturing teams to act on abnormal machine behaviour much faster. content: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan today urged Pakistan to increase imports of Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceutical products to reduce the bilateral trade imbalance and expand economic cooperation between the two countries. He made the call during a meeting with Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider at the BGMEA office in the city, said a press release. At the meeting, the BGMEA president also emphasised increasing imports of chemicals and dyes from Pakistan for Bangladesh’s garment industry, highlighting the potential for expanding trade in both directions. Although Bangladesh imports a significant volume of goods from Pakistan, including raw materials for the garment industry, its exports to the neighbouring country remain comparatively low, the release said. The BGMEA president called for greater efforts to address the imbalance by exploring new export opportunities and strengthening commercial ties. Pakistan high commissioner expressed keen interest in the proposals and assured that necessary steps would be taken to promote bilateral trade. The meeting also discussed arranging visits by high-level business delegations from both countries to identify new opportunities and establish direct commercial links. Haider said the Pakistan High Commission would facilitate business-to-business meetings and matchmaking sessions with leading Pakistani importers, brands, buyers and business associations if a Bangladeshi delegation comprising garment and other sector exporters visited Pakistan. Both sides also exchanged views on expanding market access and exploring a possible bilateral preferential trade arrangement to sustain trade flows after Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country

summary: BGMEA hosted an introductory session on 30 September for representatives from member factories to learn more about the BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate. The pilot aims to help participating factories prepare for the growing demand for transparent, verifiable production and traceability data, particularly as the […] The post BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: BGMEA hosted an introductory session on 30 September for representatives from member factories to learn more about the BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate. The pilot aims to help participating factories prepare for the growing demand for transparent, verifiable production and traceability data, particularly as the EU moves toward Digital Product Passport requirements for textiles. Through the pilot, participating factories can explore a verified, producer-owned record of production data, supported by AWARE’s Crypto TC technology. The model is designed to provide a single source of verified information that can be shared across buyer relationships, while keeping production data under the factory’s ownership. The pilot also offers guided onboarding and training, data collection and DPP creation, review and validation, with the DPP creation cost fully covered during the pilot period. The session provided factory representatives with an opportunity to better understand the pilot, its potential benefits, participation process and how digital traceability can support the Bangladesh RMG sector’s transition toward greater transparency and EU market readiness. BGMEA looks forward to supporting member factories in exploring practical digital solutions that can strengthen traceability, transparency and competitiveness in the evolving global apparel landscape. content: The rapid adoption of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is beginning to have a measurable impact on the fashion industry, changing clothing sizes, purchasing patterns and even the balance between online and physical retail. Drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro are already being associated with what has been dubbed the ‘Ozempic economy’, as significant changes in body weight force consumers to replace clothing and reconsider what and how they buy. Research from PwC suggests the impact on apparel could be substantial. Some 73% of US GLP-1 users surveyed reported a meaningful change in clothing size, while apparel spending was 9.9% higher after users had been taking the drugs for six-to-eight months. The effects are also becoming apparent in the UK. PwC estimates that around three million British adults currently use GLP-1 medications, with 40% of users surveyed saying they were spending more on clothing. One consequence could be an unexpected revival in physical clothes shopping. A US survey of 500 GLP-1 users by returns management specialist ReturnPro found that 69% had become less confident about online sizing as their bodies changed, making the ability to try garments on in stores more important. Some 71% said they were buying more apparel as their size changed, while 58% reported increased spending on premium or higher-priced clothing. More than half expected their clothing expenditure to rise further once their weight had stabilised. The trend presents challenges as well as opportunities for retailers. content: Young Labels Ltd and Japan-based Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd have started local production of the FasBano’k garment tagging system in Bangladesh, expanding the availability of the Japanese-developed technology for the country’s apparel and textile industry. The system and its local production were presented at an opening ceremony held yesterday (25 September) at the Bangla-Bano’k factory in Dhaka, bringing together representatives from Japanese organisations, Toska-Bano’k and Young Labels, according to a press release. Embassy of Japan in Bangladesh First Secretary Saori Fujimoto; Daisuke Arai of Jetro Dhaka; Yasuyuki Marahashi of Jica; Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd President Masao Terunuma; and Young Labels Ltd Managing Director S Mahmud (Mujbik) attended the event. FasBano’k is designed to attach tags using a dedicated hand tool together with specially designed tag loops or string fasteners. The system provides an alternative to conventional processes in which workers manually string or tie individual tags during garment finishing. Toska-Bano’k says its fastening mechanism allows tags to be attached more quickly than conventional manual methods, with the system designed for continuous operation. The technology can be used for garments, footwear and other textile products. Material options The tagging system is available with a range of material options, including recycled plastic, polyester, cotton, jute and paper. The different material choices allow manufacturers and brands to select tagging materials according to product specifications, sourcing requirements and sustainability considerations. For applications using recycled materials, Transaction Certificates (TCs) can also be provided where applicable for buyers and manufacturers requiring documentation relating to recycled content

The company’s performance reflects a strategy that is increasingly focused not simply on adding production volumes but on building a more diversified, integrated and flexible global manufacturing platform. title: BGMEA calls for expanded two-way trade with Pakistan
summary: Mahmud Hasan Khan, President of BGMEA, has urged Pakistan to import more Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceuticals. He said this would help reduce the trade imbalance and strengthen bilateral economic...
content: Mahmud Hasan Khan, President of BGMEA, has urged Pakistan to import more Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceuticals. He said this would help reduce the trade imbalance and strengthen bilateral economic ties. He made the call during a meeting with Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider at the BGMEA office in Dhaka, according to a press release. During the meeting, Mahmud Hasan Khan also called for greater imports of chemicals and dyes from Pakistan for Bangladesh’s garment industry, highlighting opportunities to expand trade in both directions. Bangladesh currently imports a significant volume of products from Pakistan, including raw materials used in the garment sector, while its exports to the Pakistani market remain comparatively low. The BGMEA president stressed the need to address this imbalance by identifying new export opportunities and strengthening commercial links between businesses in the two countries. The Pakistan high commissioner expressed interest in the proposals and assured that necessary steps would be taken to promote bilateral trade. The two sides also discussed arranging visits by high-level business delegations from Bangladesh and Pakistan to identify new business opportunities and establish direct commercial connections. Haider said the Pakistan High Commission would facilitate business-to-business meetings and matchmaking sessions with leading Pakistani importers, brands, buyers and business associations if a Bangladeshi delegation comprising garment and other sector exporters visits Pakistan. The meeting also focused on expanding market access and exploring a possible bilateral preferential trade arrangement to sustain trade flows after Bangladesh graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category. summary: The Japan-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JBCCI) has elected a new 16-member Board of Directors for the 2026–2028 term, with Kazuiki Kataoka taking charge as president. The new board was...
content: The Japan-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JBCCI) has elected a new 16-member Board of Directors for the 2026–2028 term, with Kazuiki Kataoka taking charge as president. The new board was formally introduced at the chamber’s 21st Annual General Meeting (AGM) held on 4th October at Hotel Lakeshore in Dhaka. Around 240 general members, board members, and distinguished guests from different organisations attended the meeting, which was moderated by JBCCI Executive Director Tahera Ahsan . The election was held on September 23, 2026, with the newly elected office bearers set to serve for the 2026–2028 term. Outgoing President Tareq Rafi Bhuiyan welcomed the participants and spoke about JBCCI’s role in promoting trade and business relations between Bangladesh and Japan. During the AGM, Former Secretary General Maria Howlader FCA presented the chamber’s major activities from November 2025 to September 2026. She said JBCCI’s membership had increased to 391 companies , compared with 369 in the previous year. The rise in membership reflects continued business engagement between companies from Bangladesh and Japan, she said. Former Joint Treasurer Md Jahangir Alam Sharker CPA presented the audited annual financial report. He said the chamber maintained sustainable financial growth while giving attention to transparency, accountability and financial management. The AGM also welcomed new members and approved the appointment of Shafiq Mizan Rahman & Augustine, Chartered Accountants , as the auditor for the 2026–27 financial year. New leadership takes charge Under the new board, Abu Zaman Md. Tariqul Islam and Syed Samiul Huq have been elected vice-presidents, while Rabiul Alam will serve as secretary general. content: On 30 September 2026, a team from Jhpiego Bangladesh paid a courtesy visit to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) to explore opportunities for collaboration in promoting the health, wellbeing, and productivity of RMG workers. The meeting was attended by BGMEA Directors — Fahima Akter and and Rumana Rashid and former BGMEA Director Md. Nazrul Islam, who engaged with the Jhpiego Bangladesh team in a constructive discussion on potential areas of collaboration. The delegation also met with BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan. Jhpiego, a global non-profit health organization and an affiliate of Johns Hopkins University, works to improve the health of women, families, and communities worldwide. Drawing on its experience in the RMG sector, the Jhpiego team shared valuable insights from its programs and study findings, highlighting the important connection between workers’ health, wellbeing, and workplace productivity. Representing Jhpiego Bangladesh were Samiha Yunus, Team Lead – Surveillance, Gazi Md. Rezaul Karim, Program Director – SRHR, Md. Afzal Hossain, Program Specialist and Farzana Khan, Private Sector Engagement Manager. The discussion explored potential avenues for partnership that can help strengthen worker-focused health initiatives and contribute to healthier workers, more productive workplaces, and more resilient factory communities. summary: Kalypso's retail consulting lead on why trust in AI should be measured by whether a decision gets better, not by whether people believe the algorithm. The post All About AI: Joshua Young of Kalypso appeared first on The Interline .
content: Originally released in The Interline’s AI Report 2026 , this executive interview with Kalypso is one of a 17-part series that sees The Interline quiz executives from companies who have either introduced new AI solutions or added meaningful new AI capabilities into their existing platforms . For more exclusive interviews, stories and opinions from different industry perspectives, and real survey feedback from voices from every level of fashion, download The AI Report 2026 . We’re observing a big disconnect (in both our own fashion-only data and in wider benchmarks from other sources) between the increasing capability and reliability of AI, in both a general sense and in discrete applications, and the lack of trust that end users place in its outputs. What do you think trust in AI looks like, and what’s the right rubric for measuring it? At its best, fashion is human, physical, emotional, and cultural. Being worn on the body, it can create performance, beauty, identity, or all three at once. It can be the Gucci Fashion Show taking over Times Square, with the noise, traffic, billboards, celebrity, commerce, and chaos of New York moving around it. Fashion can be precise and out of control at the same time. That contrast is part of the magic. The outfits are important, but so is the world they enter, the people wearing them, and the meaning a brand creates around them. That is why AI-generated fashion can feel uncomfortable. When people see synthetic models or products that feel assembled by algorithms, they can sense the absence of human intent. It may be technically impressive, but it can still feel emotionally lacking. But I do not think that is the most useful way to frame AI’s role in fashion. summary: North Wales manufacturer KnitMesh Technologies is taking its specialist wire knitting technology into the rapidly developing counter-drone market with a stainless steel mesh designed to provide a physical barrier against hostile unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The company showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at the Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe conference in London on September 30 and […] The post Knitted mesh provides physical shield against drones appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: North Wales manufacturer KnitMesh Technologies is taking its specialist wire knitting technology into the rapidly developing counter-drone market with a stainless steel mesh designed to provide a physical barrier against hostile unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The company showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at the Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe conference in London on September 30 and October 1, positioning the technology as a passive addition to the electronic detection and jamming systems increasingly being deployed to protect sensitive sites. Established in 1957 and headquartered in Greenfield, Flintshire, KnitMesh Technologies has spent almost 70 years developing knitted wire mesh for applications ranging from automotive components and filtration to hydrogen production, thermal management and industrial safety. It also operates a manufacturing facility near New Delhi, India. Developed, manufactured and tested in the UK, DroneStop employs high-strength stainless steel knitted wire mesh to create a lightweight physical barrier above or around vulnerable assets. Unlike electronic counter-drone systems, it requires no power supply and does not rely on radio-frequency interference or signal jamming. Instead, the mesh is intended to form the final physical layer of a broader counter-UAS strategy, protecting locations including military bases, ammunition and fuel storage areas, aircraft facilities, communications infrastructure, prisons and other critical national infrastructure. The approach reflects the increasing complexity of protecting sites against relatively small and inexpensive unmanned aircraft. content: Eight categories, a new Jury Board and automatic nominations for exhibiting factories put measurable impact at the center of Bangladesh’s second Textile Innovation Award. Bangladesh has spent decades proving that it can manufacture for the world. Its textile and garment industry has built global scale through speed, efficiency and production expertise. The next challenge is to capture more value from its own ideas i.e., improvements that solve real problems, deliver measurable results and can be replicated beyond a single factory. The Textile Innovation Award 2026 puts that ambition in focus. Figure: The first edition of Textile Innovation Award held in 2024. The second edition will be presented on 13 November 2026, from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM, at Hall 5 of the International Convention City Bashundhara (ICCB), Dhaka, on the second day of the TIE–ITET Textile Innovation Expo 2026 , which runs from 12–14 November in collaboration with ITET. The award is presented by Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) , in association with BKMEA and BGBA, and implemented by Textile Today Innovation Hub. The inaugural award, held on 26 October 2024, recognized Urmi Group for product development, Shasha Denims for marketing and market development, Masco Group for garment processing, and Coats Bangladesh for HR and organizational development. ATM Mahbubul Alam Chowdhury, Executive Director, Masco captured the initiative’s wider ambition in a simple phrase: “Innovation is a culture.” This year, the award covers eight categories: Process Innovation; Manufacturing Innovation; Technology; Product Development; Marketing and Market Development; Environmental Sustainability; Social Sustainability; and HR and Organizational Development. content: The Bangladesh Garment Buying House Association (BGBA) successfully held its 3rd Standing Committee Meeting on 3 October 2026 at the BGBA office. The meeting was chaired by BGBA President Md. Abdul Hamid and attended by the Chairmen, Co-Chairmen, and Members of the Standing Committees . The meeting was facilitated through a structured and coordinated session moderated by Vice President (Admin) Md. Roman Mia , ensuring focused discussion, active participation, and an effective exchange of perspectives among the Standing Committee representatives. The meeting focused on identifying and acknowledging the current challenges faced by BGBA and its members, with the objective of gaining practical insights from the Standing Committee representatives and understanding the issues from different departmental perspectives. During the session, Committee Members shared their observations, experiences, and views on the challenges encountered in their respective areas of responsibility. The discussions provided an important platform for bringing practical field-level issues to the attention of the Association and creating a clearer understanding of the areas requiring attention and collective action. BGBA believes that effective communication, collective participation, and practical recommendations from its Standing Committees are essential to addressing emerging challenges and strengthening the Association’s services and activities. The Association remains committed to working collaboratively with its Standing Committees and members to develop practical approaches, strengthen member support, and ensure more effective and coordinated initiatives for the continued progress of BGBA and the RMG Buying House sector. title: Germany’s apparel market remains under pressure
summary: Germany’s apparel market experienced notable pressure in 2026, driven by a broader contraction in European clothing imports and surging domestic energy costs. Provisional Eurostat data shows Germany’s...
content: Germany’s apparel market experienced notable pressure in 2026, driven by a broader contraction in European clothing imports and surging domestic energy costs. Provisional Eurostat data shows Germany’s clothing imports from non-EU suppliers fell 17.0% year-over-year in the first half of 2026. Figure: In fiscal year 2025–26, garment exports to Germany totaled $4.38 billion, highlighting the market’s ongoing scale. This downturn coincides with sharp cost increases across the German trade landscape. According to the Federal Statistical Office, import prices jumped 8.3% year-over-year in August 2026, marking the sharpest annual surge since December 2022. Export prices also climbed 4.7% during the same month. A 43.0% spike in imported energy costs served as the primary catalyst for these inflationary pressures. The weakening demand extends beyond Germany to the broader European market. Total EU apparel imports from global suppliers dropped 9.7% year-over-year to €41.1 billion during the first six months of 2026. Import volumes shrank by 6.4%, while average unit prices declined by 3.53%. Despite tightening market conditions, Germany maintains its position as a major European hub for international apparel trade. In fiscal year 2025–26, garment exports to Germany totaled $4.38 billion, highlighting the market’s ongoing scale. Moving forward, dynamic cost structures, shifting consumer demand, and fluctuating energy prices will remain critical factors shaping Germany’s global supply chains and trade stability.

content: Wendler Interlining Bangladesh Limited officially opened its new production facility in Bangladesh on Saturday, marking a significant milestone in the German textile specialist’s long-term commitment to the country’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry. The opening ceremony brought together senior executives of Wendler Interlining Group, industry stakeholders and business partners to celebrate the company’s growing presence in Bangladesh and its vision for the future of the global interlining market. Wendler Interlining, a family-owned German company with roots dating back to 1843, has evolved from a textile finisher into a specialist in high-quality interlinings for the garment industry. The company established its own Bangladesh subsidiary in 2022, building on its production presence in the country since 2009. According to the company, Bangladesh is a strategically important market because of its position as one of the world’s largest garment-producing countries. From 180 years of heritage to a new chapter in Bangladesh: Addressing the ceremony, Dr Gerhart Wendler, Chairman of Wendler Interlining Group, highlighted the company’s long history, its transformation through successive generations and its continuing commitment to innovation and quality. He spoke about Wendler’s journey from its establishment in 1843 to becoming an international specialist in interlinings. The company shifted its strategic focus to high-quality interlining fabrics in 1974 and subsequently expanded its presence across major garment-producing markets in Asia. Dr Wendler also outlined the group’s future ambition of strengthening its position as the market leader in interlinings, with Bangladesh playing an increasingly important role in that strategy. title: Rooftop solar offers a lifeline for Bangladesh RMG sector
summary: Bangladesh’s apparel sector is installing rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems to handle severe gas shortages and grid failures. Reliable electricity is necessary to protect export production. Rooftop so...
content: Bangladesh’s apparel sector is installing rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems to handle severe gas shortages and grid failures. Reliable electricity is necessary to protect export production. Rooftop solar helps factory owners produce clean energy, lower power costs, and run uninterrupted operations. Assessing industrial rooftop capacity and demand impact The potential for solar generation across the apparel manufacturing landscape is substantial. A detailed assessment by the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) reveals that 3,320 garment factories across the country possess a cumulative rooftop solar potential of 1,768 megawatt-peak (MWp). The study mapped roughly 9.7 million square meters of usable rooftop area. Under optimal setup, solar arrays can meet a median of 39.9% of electricity demand in large factories, 33.1% in medium-sized units, and 38% in small manufacturing facilities. Converting this potential into active capacity requires structured investment. Recent Report data identifies 509 factories as investment-ready, with another 1,359 factories capable of becoming investable with financial support. Installing rooftop systems across 2,303 non-solar factories requires an estimated total investment of $188.2 million. Expanding factory adoption and portfolio targets Factory-level solar deployments are expanding rapidly through experienced engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) providers. Solaric, a major industrial solar installer, reports a portfolio target of 212 MWp in total installations for 2025, which is projected to expand to 400 MWp by 2027. content: Raidha Collections Ltd., one of the largest sister concerns of Labib Group, has appointed its new CEO, Shazia Zaheen Alamgir, daughter of Salahuddin Alamgir and Sultana Jahan, Chairman and Vice Chairman of Labib Group. She has been appointed Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Raidha Collections and has taken charge of the role. Shazia Zaheen Alamgir has been associated with the group’s business activities for a long time as Group Director. During her tenure as Director, she gained experience in Labib Group’s management and business operations. She completed her MYP diploma and IB diploma at International School Dhaka (ISD). She subsequently earned her undergraduate degree from Emerson College in Boston, USA, and her postgraduate degree from City St. george’s, University of London. In her new role, Shazia Zaheen Alamgir will lead overall business operations, with a strong focus on EU business and management of Raidha Collections. At the same time, she will work to further advance the company’s business growth and future initiatives. In her personal life, she is married to Siraajam Munir Khan. Both are associated with City, St George’s, University of London. Siraajam Munir Khan is the son of Ikram Ahmed Khan, Chairman of the Dubai- and Hong Kong-based Shun Shing Group. Labib Group and its associates extend their warm congratulations to Shazia Zaheen Alamgir and wish her continued success in her new role. title: Rampal power plant sets new record with 1,321MW generation
summary: The Rampal coal-fired power plant in Bagerhat has generated a record 1,321 megawatts (MW) of electricity, exceeding its combined installed capacity of 1,320MW. At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 g...
content: The Rampal coal-fired power plant in Bagerhat has generated a record 1,321 megawatts (MW) of electricity, exceeding its combined installed capacity of 1,320MW. At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 generated 656MW while Unit 2 produced 665MW, bringing the plant’s total generation to 1,321MW. Figure: At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 generated 656MW while Unit 2 produced 665MW, bringing the plant’s total generation to 1,321MW. According to Anwarul Azim, General Manager of the Rampal Thermal Power Plant, both units are supplying electricity directly to Bangladesh's national grid. “After production was temporarily suspended due to a mechanical fault, the two units are now generating electricity continuously,” he said. He added that electricity from the plant would be supplied to the national grid according to demand. The Rampal power plant, located in Bagerhat, was initiated as a joint venture between Bangladesh and India in 2010. The latest generation milestone comes after both units resumed operations following a mechanical fault, allowing the plant to supply electricity continuously to the national grid.

Organized jointly by WaterAid Bangladesh and BKMEA with support from the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka, the program brought together […] The post BKMEA inaugurated its Water Cell to strengthen the industry’s role in responsible water management appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: BKMEA inaugurated its Water Cell yesterday (3 October 2026) to strengthen the industry’s role in responsible water management. The inauguration was held alongside an awareness and consultation session on Water Stewardship in Bangladesh’s knitwear sector. Organized jointly by WaterAid Bangladesh and BKMEA with support from the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka, the program brought together representatives from the knitwear industry, BKMEA and international brands. BKMEA Director Engr. Md. Belayet Hossain represented BKMEA during the inaugural session. The day-long program featured technical discussions and group activities on measuring and reducing water consumption, increasing water reuse and preventing pollution, along with exploring opportunities to develop water-efficiency initiatives into viable and investment-ready projects. In his closing remarks, BKMEA Executive President Ehsan Fazlee Shamim emphasized that water management should not be viewed solely from a business perspective; it is also an ethical responsibility. He highlighted that the impacts of water misuse and pollution ultimately affect our country, communities and people, making responsible water use a collective responsibility. The initiative is expected to strengthen awareness, capacity and collaboration on responsible water management across Bangladesh’s knitwear sector. title: Govt targets higher-value jute products to boost export earnings
summary: The government is working to boost the value of locally produced jute by promoting value‑added products. The goal is to increase foreign exchange earnings, raise revenue, and expand both domestic and...
content: The government is working to boost the value of locally produced jute by promoting value‑added products. The goal is to increase foreign exchange earnings, raise revenue, and expand both domestic and global markets. Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Minister of Textiles and Jute, made the remarks while inaugurating a six-day Versatile Jute Products Fair and a new sales outlet, JDPC Express, at the Jute Diversification Promotion Center (JDPC) in Tejgaon, Dhaka. Figure: Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Minister of Textiles and Jute made the remarks while inaugurating a six-day Versatile Jute Products Fair and a new sales outlet, JDPC Express. Khandakar Abdul Muktadir also said, the government is developing a plan in coordination with the JDPC and private-sector entrepreneurs to promote value addition across the jute industry. He said converting raw jute into products such as sliver, packaging materials and blended fibers could significantly increase its market value. According to the minister, a tone of raw jute, which reached around Tk150,000, or about $1,200, at peak market prices last year, could generate $2,400–2,500 when processed into packaging products. Notably, the value could rise further to around $4,000–5,000 per ton when jute is converted into higher-value products, including blended fibers made by combining jute with cotton or other fibers. The government aims to process the maximum possible share of domestically produced jute into value-added products, he said. content: Author: Sultan Mahmud Sohal, Country Manager, Corporate Responsibility, KM International GmbH (Branch office of FLORETT TEXTIL GmbH & Co. KG) Ten years is long enough to change an industry, and it is certainly long enough to leave an imprint on the people who work within it. In Bangladesh, the story of garments and textiles is often presented through export earnings, factory numbers, production capacity, employment and market share. These figures are important because they demonstrate the extraordinary scale of an industry that has become central to the country’s economy and international identity. Yet numbers alone cannot capture what this sector really represents. Behind every shipment is a worker beginning a shift, an engineer solving a production problem, a merchandiser managing a demanding deadline, an entrepreneur taking a financial risk, a technician learning a new machine, or a young professional trying to build a career in an industry that connects Bangladesh with consumers across the world. Behind every factory is a community, and behind every export figure are millions of individual stories. That human dimension is what makes Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry much more than an economic statistic. It is an important part of the country’s social and economic transformation, and for the past ten years, Textile Focus has been one of the dedicated platforms telling that story. summary: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments...
content: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments. They are usually made from materials like plastic, metal, shell, wood, or resin. Plastic buttons, such as those made from ABS, polyester, and nylon, are popular because they are inexpensive, durable, and easy to design. However, these synthetic materials contribute to microplastic pollution, release harmful chemicals during production, and do not break down naturally. This raises serious environmental concerns [1]. With around 60 billion buttons produced each year, even a slight change to sustainable materials can significantly impact the environment [2] At the same time, the textile and fashion industries significantly harm the environment. They contribute to solid textile waste. Textile Solid Waste (TSW) is categorized into pre-consumer, production, and post-consumer waste. The textile sector generates nearly 5% of all global waste, while millions of tonnes of textile waste are generated and disposed of in landfills each year. [3]. This study explores making composite buttons using waste fabric, wood sawdust, and ETP sludge, with epoxy resin as the binder using the Hand Lay-Up method. Findings show that these waste-based composites could serve as a sustainable and functional alternative to traditional plastic buttons in the textile industry Objectives The goal of this project is to create sustainable composite buttons using leftover textiles and assess how well they work for real-world uses. title: Sedex expands supply chain mapping beyond Tier 1
summary: Sedex has upgraded its supply chain sustainability platform to give companies deeper visibility into suppliers beyond Tier 1. The update comes as companies face growing pressure to identify risks acr...
content: Sedex has upgraded its supply chain sustainability platform to give companies deeper visibility into suppliers beyond Tier 1. The update comes as companies face growing pressure to identify risks across extended supply chains. Sedex’s sample survey found that only 12% of organizations have data from most of their second-tier suppliers. Sedex data shows another gap. About 15% of supply chain worksites have no measures to ensure their suppliers or subcontractors meet required labor standards. The new mapping workflow allows suppliers to add and label upstream connections by tier. The platform also gives buying organizations more detailed risk intelligence. Analytics dashboards can identify higher-risk suppliers by tier and highlight gaps in risk mitigation. Sedex has expanded its risk assessment tools across 15 topics for more than 120,000 registered worksites. The Audit Risk pillar uses findings from more than 250,000 SMETA audits across 115,000 sites in 106 countries. It also incorporates data from the latest SMETA 7.0 standard. Sedex has also upgraded its Wages Risk pillar. It combines wage data from more than 70,000 site-level SMETA audits with external expert sources. A new environmental risk assessment feature brings environmental data together at the worksite level. This can help companies prioritize environmental due diligence across their supplier networks.

title: Patagonia joins ACT to push living wages across apparel supply chains
summary: Patagonia has joined the ACT Initiative, strengthening its focus on living wages through industry-wide collaboration and collective bargaining. Patagonia defines a living wage as income that allows w...
content: Patagonia has joined the ACT Initiative, strengthening its focus on living wages through industry-wide collaboration and collective bargaining. Patagonia defines a living wage as income that allows workers to meet basic needs such as food, housing, healthcare, and education. In many apparel-producing countries, statutory minimum wages remain below these levels. The company has worked on living wages for more than a decade. In 2015, Patagonia set a goal for all workers across its supply chain to earn a living wage by 2025. It also researched wage gaps, worked with suppliers, and introduced programs to support workers. These included supplier education, wage assessments, and Fair Trade mechanisms that provided direct financial benefits to workers. However, Patagonia now says broader economic and policy factors also shape wage outcomes. “For years, our focus was on the actions we could take directly with suppliers and their workers,” said Wendy Savage, Senior Director of Social Impact and Transparency at Patagonia. “What we’ve learned is that lasting wage growth depends on much broader systems, including government policies and industry-wide agreements.” The ACT Initiative, which stands for Action, Collaboration, Transformation, brings together brands, retailers, employer organizations, governments, and the IndustriALL Global Union. Patagonia’s move therefore shifts its living wage strategy from mainly supplier-level programs toward broader industry and country-level action.

content: Bangladesh's business and trade sectors are currently navigating various changes and challenges. The private sector is confronting a harsh reality shaped by factors such as the energy crisis, high interest rates, financing constraints, bureaucratic complexities, and the overall investment climate. Looming ahead are significant challenges, including graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) status, new trade agreements, the need to retain export markets, and the imperative to diversify products within the garment industry. Figure: Md. Fazlul Hoque, Administrator of the FBCCI and Managing Director of Plummy Fashions Ltd. Against this backdrop, Md. Fazlul Hoque, Administrator of the FBCCI, recently spoke with Textile Today. He is the Managing Director of Plummy Fashions Ltd. and previously served as the President of the BKMEA. He is also a member of the Board of Directors of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), Bangladesh. Drawing on his extensive experience in the business and industrial sectors, he discussed critical issues facing the country's trade and commerce, including the energy crisis, investment, LDC graduation, Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), diversification in the garment industry, worker wages, and FBCCI elections. Textile Today: What do you consider to be the biggest challenges currently facing businesses in Bangladesh? Md. Fazlul Hoque: Doing business in a developing country like Bangladesh involves constantly facing new challenges. Currently, one of the major issues is energy supply. content: Saurer Texparts held an ‘In‑Mill Product’ symposium with Saiham Group in Habiganj, Bangladesh. The event brought 45 participants for technical training on its latest spinning components and solutions. The initiative highlighted Saurer Texparts’ focus on direct customer engagement and the practical application of technical knowledge in spinning mills. Led by M Gopi, Global Sales Manager, Saurer Textile Solutions Private Ltd ., the symposium provided participants with technical insights into solutions designed to improve energy efficiency, yarn quality and productivity in spinning operations. Among the technologies discussed was the Spinnfinity and E-Shape spindle, which can reduce energy consumption by up to 6%. The session also covered the PK 2360 SEH, featuring a robust mechanical system with a hexagonal support rod aimed at enhancing yarn quality in spinning machines. Another key solution presented was the RB 105 rotor bearing system, which uses advanced materials to support higher productivity in rotor spinning operations. The training was designed to move beyond theoretical product knowledge by demonstrating how the technologies can be assessed under actual mill conditions. Figure: M Gopi, Global Sales Manager, Saurer Textile Solutions Private Ltd . Following the symposium, Saiham Group is evaluating Texparts solutions in real production environments to assess their performance and suitability for its spinning operations. According to Saurer Texparts, the initiative created an opportunity for technical knowledge exchange while allowing the company to better understand customer requirements and support mills in improving operational performance. title: Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition targets scale-up of lower-carbon
summary: The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has launched with more than 60 fashion brands, retailers, manufacturers, and innovators to accelerate the commercial adoption of lower-carbon materials and product...
content: The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has launched with more than 60 fashion brands, retailers, manufacturers, and innovators to accelerate the commercial adoption of lower-carbon materials and production technologies. Figure: Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition will focus on organic, recycled, and next-generation fibers. The coalition was launched on September 23, 2026, by The Climate Pledge, Amazon, Stella McCartney and Canopy, with convening support from the World Economic Forum. It aims to address one of fashion’s biggest sustainability barriers. This moves proven solutions from small-scale innovation to commercial production. The initiative will focus on organic, recycled and next-generation fibers. It will also support manufacturing technologies that can reduce water use, chemical inputs and greenhouse gas emissions. According to Global Fashion Agenda and McKinsey, the fashion industry generated about 2.1 billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. Around 70% came from upstream activities such as materials production, preparation and processing. The coalition is therefore targeting the supply chain earlier in the product lifecycle instead of focusing mainly on garment reuse, recycling and disposal. The initiative builds on the wider Climate Pledge network, which now includes more than 700 signatories across more than 60 industries. Its members are committed to reaching net-zero carbon by 2040. Fashion-focused participants include Anna Sui, Another Tomorrow, Bananatex, Brooks Running, Circ, DL1961, E.L.V Denim, Mother Denim, Selfridges, unspun and Vestiaire Collective. For fashion manufacturers, this could gradually expand access to lower-impact fibers and technologies beyond limited pilot projects.

title: Stakeholders’ Dialogue on Ending Digital & AI-Facilitated Violence Against Women
summary: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Stakeholders’ Dialogue and Preparatory Workshop on Ending Digital Violence Against Women, held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon, brought together policymakers, parliamentarians and civil society leaders to address the rapidly growing threat of AI-enabled harassment, abuse and exploitation of women and children. The session was moderated by Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asad […] The post Stakeholders’ Dialogue on Ending Digital & AI-Facilitated Violence Against Women appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Stakeholders’ Dialogue and Preparatory Workshop on Ending Digital Violence Against Women, held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon, brought together policymakers, parliamentarians and civil society leaders to address the rapidly growing threat of AI-enabled harassment, abuse and exploitation of women and children. The session was moderated by Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asad Alam Siam, with remarks from Hon’ble State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ms. Shama Obaed Islam, MP; Hon’ble State Minister for Social Welfare Ms. Farzana Sharmin Putul, MP; Hon’ble Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Md. Asaduzzaman, MP; Barrister Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, MP; and Ms. Sanjida Islam Tulee, MP. Speaking at the dialogue, Vidiya Amrit Khan, Vice President, BGMEA, stressed that addressing digital and AI-facilitated violence must begin with a broader change in society, culture and mindset towards women. She highlighted the silence surrounding domestic and child sexual abuse, the social taboos that prevent survivors from seeking help, and the urgent need for stronger implementation of existing laws. She called for educating children from an early age to respect women and recognise their value, alongside stronger enforcement, AI safeguards and age-appropriate regulation of children’s access to social media. She further emphasised that, as a Muslim woman, she believes Islam unequivocally upholds the dignity, rights and respect of women. The meeting was part of Bangladesh government’s work to establish the Dhaka Dialogue, a government-led platform introduced at the 10th Dakar International Forum on Peace and Security in Africa on 20 April 2026. content: At a CCEA meeting on Thursday, the government gave final approval to a draft 15-year concession agreement with an international terminal operator. The government has decided to hand over the operation and maintenance of Chattogram Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its overflow yard (OCY) to a foreign operator. At a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury on Thursday, final approval was given to a draft 15-year concession agreement with an international terminal operator. According to a proposal submitted by the Ministry of Shipping, Chattogram Port Authority (CPA) will sign the agreement under a project titled “Operation and Maintenance of Chattogram Port Authority’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and Overflow Yard (OCY)” under a public-private partnership (PPP) project. Meanwhile, the CCEA gave in-principle approval to another proposal submitted by the industries ministry. content: From pioneering India’s Overhead Travelling Cleaner more than five decades ago to developing intelligent automation systems for modern spinning mills, ELGI Electric is now making automation the next major chapter in its engineering journey. V.S. Balasubramanian, President-Operations , ELGI Electric “Whenever we introduced a new product, we never compromised on technology. We first identified the best technology available anywhere in the world and then worked towards making it even better for Indian customers. That philosophy has remained unchanged throughout our journey.” This philosophy perhaps best explains both the longevity of ELGI Electric Industries Ltd. and the direction in which the Coimbatore-based engineering company is now heading. For more than six decades, ELGI Electric has built its reputation by identifying emerging technologies, adapting them to Indian textile manufacturing and continuously refining them in close collaboration with customers. Its pioneering introduction of the Overhead Travelling Cleaner (OHTC) to India established the company’s position in textile machinery. Subsequent developments in yarn conditioning, fire and metal detection and Bobbin Transportation Systems expanded that engineering base. Today, however, the opportunity is considerably larger. As textile manufacturing becomes increasingly automated, connected and data-driven, ELGI Electric is moving beyond individual machines towards integrated automation solutions that connect processes, reduce manual intervention and improve productivity. The shift is being driven by a fundamental change in the industry’s requirements. summary: 언노운네이처의 착색 케어 브랜드 아윌미백은 우주글로벌과 중국 총판 계약을 체결했다.아윌미백 측에 따르면 ‘뱀파이어 톤업 스프레이’는 지난 7월 중국 왕홍 따따의 라이브 방송에서 준비 물량이 약 2시간 만에 소진됐다. 브랜드는 해당 기간 더우인 주간 판매 1위를 기록했으며 이후 수만 개 단위 추가 물량을 현지에 공급했다고 밝혔다.우주글로벌은 지난 6월부터 해당 제품의 중국 물량 공급을 담당해 왔으며 이번 계약을 통해 공식 총판 역할을 맡는다. 양사는 온라인 판매를 중심으로 유통을 운영한 뒤 오프라인 채널까지 단계적으로 확대할 계획이다

title: Six forces reweaving the future of global textiles
title_ko: 글로벌 섬유의 미래를 엮는 6가지 힘
summary: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and...
content: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and made polyester the workhorse of modern textiles. But the formula is changing. Global fiber production reached a record 132 million tons in 2024 , up from around 125 million tons in 2023. Production has more than doubled since 2000 and under business-as-usual conditions could reach approximately 169 million tons by 2030 . Courtesy: Collected The industry is being pushed to use different materials, reduce waste, automate production, prove its claims and build supply chains that can withstand disruption. Six forces are changing this transition: man-made fibers, circularity, AI and automation, traceability, supply-chain regionalization and advanced materials. Together, they are rewriting the economics of textiles. MMFs If one fiber defines the modern textile economy, it is polyester. Polyester represented around 59% of global fiber production in 2024 , with output rising from approximately 71 million tons in 2023 to about 78 million tons in 2024. Yet around 88% of polyester remained fossil-based . That creates one of the industry's biggest contradictions. Sustainability ambitions are growing while dependence on virgin synthetic materials continues to increase. Replacing polyester entirely is unlikely to happen quickly. Its durability, affordability, versatility and performance have made it indispensable across sportswear, outerwear, home textiles and everyday apparel. Then what will the next generation of polyester be made from? title: AI Labs Keep Demoing The Weirdest Fashion Use Cases
summary: The latest marketing push into always-on AI agents featured fashion, again. But the big labs keep showcasing brand-owners and professionals who seem to want to care less and delegate everything. The more useful promise is the ability to care more: freeing time and attention to improve the product. The post AI Labs Keep Demoing The Weirdest Fashion Use Cases appeared first on The Interline .
content: [Featured image using Dots artwork for inspiration.] Key Takeaways: For the second time in as many months, OpenAI has released a new product with a fashion workflow featured prominently in the accompanying demo. These hypothetical workflows keep presenting an odd window into the reality of AI deployments and the likely real sources of ROI for actual fashion businesses, and the incentives are difficult to decipher. Market data presented by a16z and The Interline’s own survey examine different aspects of AI uptake and measurement, with some correlation showing that AI adoption needs to translate into demonstrable product outcomes – especially if agentic commerce ends up de-emphasising website visits. In a new attempt at “sherlocking,” OpenAI launched its own virtual try-on service that hooks into its own in-app shopping experiences and into the company’s new play to become users’ default operating environment. title: Bangladesh exports rise 8.54% in September as RMG shipments recover
summary: Key insights September merchandise exports rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion. RMG exports increased 8.56% to $3.08 billion, with both knitwear and woven garments posting annual growth. Septemb...
content: Key insights September merchandise exports rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion. RMG exports increased 8.56% to $3.08 billion, with both knitwear and woven garments posting annual growth. September exports fell 11.11% from August, showing weaker month-on-month momentum. RMG accounted for about 78.30% of total export earnings in September. Jute, leather and home textiles added strength to the wider export basket. Figure: Export earnings rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion from $3.63 billion in September 2025. Bangladesh’s merchandise exports maintained year-on-year growth in September, although export earnings declined sharply from the previous month. Export earnings rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion from $3.63 billion in September 2025, according to the latest Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data. RMG remains the main export engine Table 1. Bangladesh’s RMG export performance in September 2026 Category September 2025 ($ Billion) September 2026 ($ Billion) Growth Rate (YoY) Knitwear 1.86 2.02 +8.58% Woven garments 0.98 1.06 +8.54% Total RMG 2.84 3.08 +8.56% Total exports 3.63 3.94 +8.54% Source: Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) The RMG sector accounted for about 78.30% of Bangladesh’s total merchandise export earnings in September. RMG exports reached $3.08 billion, up 8.56% from $2.84 billion a year earlier. Within the sector, knitwear and woven garments both recorded year-on-year growth of 8.58% and 8.54%, respectively. The quarterly data also show that knitwear remained the larger apparel segment. During July-September, knitwear exports reached $5.96 billion, up 6.88%, while woven garment exports stood at $4.61 billion, representing 5.11% growth. Researchers estimate that synthetic fibre production in 2021 could have been 47 per cent lower [...] The post What if fast fashion never happened? appeared first on Apparel Insider .
content: HELSINKI – Global synthetic fibre production could have been almost half its current level without the rise of fast fashion. This is according to new research which used computer modelling to examine how the textile industry might otherwise have developed. Researchers estimate that synthetic fibre production in 2021 could have been 47 per cent lower without the growth associated with fast fashion.
