title: Rieter announces Daniel Lippuner as new CEO
summary: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Rieter has announced Daniel Lippuner as its new CEO. The leadership transition happened as Thomas Oetterli is stepping down from the CEO role, effective October 31...
content: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Rieter has announced Daniel Lippuner as its new CEO. The leadership transition happened as Thomas Oetterli is stepping down from the CEO role, effective October 31, 2026, and handing over the chairmanship of the company’s Board of Directors. Figure: Daniel Lippuner new CEO of Rieter Daniel Lippuner will become CEO of Rieter on November 1, 2026. He brings extensive international leadership experience and industry knowledge, particularly in textile machinery and components. Oetterli said the decision follows the successful implementation of Rieter’s Next Level performance program, structural measures to consolidate the company’s sites and the acquisition of Barmag. “After the successful implementation of the Next Level performance program, the structural measures initiated to consolidate the sites and the acquisition of Barmag, the time has come to hand over responsibility to new hands,” Oetterli said. The separation of the CEO and Board Chairman roles had been planned since Oetterli took office. Daniel previously served as CEO of the Saurer Group and headed Oerlikon Textile Components, where he was involved in businesses covering spinning machinery, yarn processing and textile components. He also served as Chairman of the Board and co-owner of Heberlein Technology, maintaining close ties with the chemical fiber industry. His experience in transformation, technology and quality management, operational leadership and Asian markets is expected to support Rieter as the company expands beyond its traditional short-staple fiber business. title: Is the biomass boiler boom creating Bangladesh’s next environmental problem?
summary: No gas, expensive diesel—Will our forests, soil, and air burn in the race for alternative fuels? Bangladesh’s industries, especially garments and textiles, face gas shortages, unreliable supplies,...
content: No gas, expensive diesel—Will our forests, soil, and air burn in the race for alternative fuels? Bangladesh’s industries, especially garments and textiles, face gas shortages, unreliable supplies, and rising energy costs. Diesel has risen from Tk 97.5 to Tk 135 per liter, natural gas costs Tk 26.09 per cubic meter excluding VAT, and LPG Tk 108 per kilogram. Many factories have already reduced production because of gas and electricity shortages. Entrepreneurs are therefore turning to LPG, diesel, and biomass boilers. But if we escape a fuel crisis by creating an environmental crisis, society will pay the price. Biomass: Solution or new crisis? Biomass boilers are spreading rapidly, especially chain-grate and fixed-grate models. Biomass could reduce fossil-fuel dependence if it uses sustainable agricultural and natural waste. The key question is: Do we have enough sustainable biomass? Installing a boiler is easy. Securing fuel for the next 10 years is much harder. Is rice husk enough? In Bangladesh, a huge amount of rice husk is used in rice bran oil manufacturing facilities and rice mills, where it is used for heating and steam generation. Biomass boilers had long been used in rice mills before being introduced to the textile industry in Bangladesh. Rice husk has a typical calorific value of about 3,000 kcal/kg, depending on its moisture content and composition. Due to its low calorific value, a huge quantity is required, which is not cost-effective. To increase the calorific value, they may mix rice husk with wood chips, sawdust, and wood. This raises a serious question: Where will the extra wood come from? Bangladesh’s forests are already under pressure. title: EURATEX calls for a harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility
summary: EURATEX has joined a broad coalition of European industry organisations calling on the upcoming Circular Economy Act to establish a stronger and more harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). In a joint position paper, the signatories underline that the Circular Economy Act should help Europe move from fragmented national waste management systems towards… Read more The post EURATEX calls for a harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility appeared first on EURATEX .
content: EURATEX has joined a broad coalition of European industry organisations calling on the upcoming Circular Economy Act to establish a stronger and more harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). In a joint position paper, the signatories underline that the Circular Economy Act should help Europe move from fragmented national waste management systems towards a functioning Single Market for secondary raw materials . Extended Producer Responsibility already plays a central role in financing the collection, sorting and recycling of waste across Europe. However, different national approaches and administrative requirements continue to create complexity for companies operating across borders and can limit the development of circular value chains. A more harmonised European approach The coalition therefore calls for a horizontal EU EPR Regulation , establishing a common baseline for EU-mandated EPR schemes while allowing sector-specific requirements where needed. Such an approach would help reduce regulatory fragmentation, provide greater legal certainty and support the scaling-up of circular business models and cross-border markets for secondary raw materials. The paper also stresses that EPR systems should remain producer-led . Producers should retain responsibility for decision-making alongside their obligation to finance end-of-life management, while public authorities provide appropriate oversight. Producer contributions should remain dedicated to the collection, sorting and recycling systems for which they were raised. Transparency, simpler rules and investment in recycling Greater transparency across the entire waste management chain is another key priority. title: The Column Skirt Anchors a Quieter Fall/Winter 2026

content: Kraig Biocraft Laboratories has shipped its first commercial order of recombinant spider silk yarn, marking a significant step towards the use of the company’s technology in performance textiles. The custom-engineered yarn was produced to fulfil a purchase commitment from an unnamed global performance sports brand and will now be developed into a new performance textile. The shipment forms part of a confidential pilot development programme targeting the athletic apparel market. Kraig Labs said the yarn has been custom processed to the customer’s specifications, with the initial volume intentionally kept small for the precision application. “Completing the delivery of this spider silk yarn is a huge milestone for Kraig Labs,” said Kim Thompson, founder and CEO of Kraig Labs. “The volume is small by design. This is a precision application, not a bulk order.” Kraig Labs’ technology uses genetically engineered silkworms incorporating key spider silk proteins to produce recombinant spider silk. The company believes the resulting combination of strength, flexibility, toughness and low weight makes the material particularly suited to demanding performance applications. The commercial shipment follows the company’s work to move its spider silk technology from development and scaled production towards customer-led textile applications. Kraig Labs sees elite performance apparel as a potentially important proving ground for the technology, where improvements in strength-to-weight ratio, durability and other material properties can translate directly into product performance. “High-performance sport is where materials prove themselves,” Thompson said. “Performance wins. Organized by the BUTEX Science Club, the day-long event will begin at 8:00 am and continue until evening. […] The post Texverse 2.0 to be held at BUTEX on October 30 appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: The Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) will host the national competition ‘Texverse 2.0’ on October 30, bringing together students from universities, textile engineering colleges, and higher secondary institutions for competitions focused on research, innovation, creativity, and problem-solving. Organized by the BUTEX Science Club, the day-long event will begin at 8:00 am and continue until evening. Different segments of the competition will be held at the university’s Auditorium, Seminar Room, Academic Building, and Central Field, while some competitions will be conducted online. The event has so far established collaboration with 25 student clubs and organizations from different universities and textile colleges across the country. These include KUET Textile Club, BUP Career Club, Textile Club-MBSTU, DUET Textile Career & Research Club, NITER Science Society, BUFT Career Development Club, Daffodil AI Club, Southeast University Textile Club (SEUTC), Green University Textile Club (GUTC), Sonargaon University Textile Club, and RTEC Research Club, among others. The competition aims to encourage students to engage in research and innovation while developing practical and sustainable solutions to challenges faced by the textile sector. It will also provide participants with a platform to showcase their creative ideas, technical knowledge, and problem-solving abilities. At the university level, the competition will feature project exhibition, research-based poster presentation, quiz competition, textile case competition, treasure hunt, essay writing and an artificial intelligence-based video-making competition. title: Tencel market heads toward $6.15 billion as lyocell demand accelerates
title_ko: lyocell 수요가 가속화됨에 따라 Tencel 시장은 61억 5천만 달러로 향합니다.
summary: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market...
content: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market was valued at $3.5 billion in 2025. It is projected to reach $6.15 billion by 2033, growing at a 7.8% CAGR from 2026 to 2033. The growth is supported by demand for sustainable materials, stronger traceability requirements and advances in fiber technology. Tencel products include Lyocell and Modal fibers, which are used across apparel, home textiles and technical applications. A separate 2026 market analysis gives a more detailed view of the fabric segment. According to PW Consulting, the Tencel fiber fabric market reached $3.67 billion in 2025 and could reach $5.94 billion by 2032, at a 7.15% CAGR. Lyocell fiber fabric held the largest share at 59.8%. Apparel remains the largest end-use segment. Apparel and clothing generated about $2.37 billion, or 64.7% of the Tencel fiber fabric market, in 2025. Home textiles followed with $927.7 million, or 25.3%. Technical textiles accounted for $365.4 million, or 10%. Asia-Pacific remains the largest regional market. It generated about $1.64 billion in Tencel fiber fabric revenue in 2025. Europe followed at $929.8 million, while North America reached $656.8 million. The broader fiber market also shows stronger demand for regenerated cellulose. According to Lenzing, global production of lyocell, modal, and viscose increased about 4% to 8.7 million tons in 2025. Lyocell and modal output increased at a double-digit rate. Technology remains a major differentiator. TENCEL™ Lyocell uses a closed-loop process that recovers more than 99.8% of the solvent. title: IFKT conference opens in Zagreb
summary: The 52nd International Conference of the International Federation of Knitting Technologists (IFKT) is taking place in Zagreb, Croatia, from 30 September to 2 October 2026, bringing together specialists from industry, academia and research. Organised by the Croatian section of IFKT in collaboration with the University of Zagreb, the international meeting combines technical presentations and poster […] The post IFKT conference opens in Zagreb appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: The 52nd International Conference of the International Federation of Knitting Technologists (IFKT) is taking place in Zagreb, Croatia, from 30 September to 2 October 2026, bringing together specialists from industry, academia and research. Organised by the Croatian section of IFKT in collaboration with the University of Zagreb, the international meeting combines technical presentations and poster sessions with opportunities for discussion and networking among knitting professionals. The conference programme began on Wednesday 30 September at the University of Zagreb Faculty of Textile Technology with a meeting of the IFKT Central Board followed by the organisation’s General Assembly. The technical conference programme opened on Thursday 1 October at Zagreb’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum. Following registration and the opening ceremony, Zlatko Vrljičak delivered the introductory lecture, Employment in the Croatian Textile and Clothing Industry: With Special Emphasis on the Knitwear Industry . The first oral session focuses on technology, materials and characterisation and is chaired by Marcus O. Weber. Among the opening presentations is Cotton Grass Fibers – Textile Technological Approach , delivered by Marc Küperkoch. Thomas Mutschler and Marc Küperkoch are also presenting research into component optimisation for high-speed yarn guiding elements designed for processing highly abrasive yarns at high speeds. The work examines ceramic materials and high-frequency vibrations. The programme continues through 2 October, with the conference providing a platform for sharing developments in knitting technology, materials, textile engineering and associated research. content: DHAKA – Bangladesh is set to quadruple polyester-chip capacity at a local producer, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported synthetic textile inputs. The move comes as garment makers seek to expand beyond cotton and move into new product segments. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has signed a US$50mloan with Modern Syntex Limited, part of TK Group, to expand its polyester-chip manufacturing operation in the Mirsarai Economic Zone near Chattogram. The project will increase the plant’s capacity from 107 tonnes to 407 tonnes a day. It is designed to produce high-intrinsic-viscosity polyester chips for higher-value textile and apparel applications, with commercial operations targeted for 2027. The investment comes as Bangladesh’s garment industry remains heavily weighted towards cotton, while manufacturers look to capture more orders for man-made-fibre products. Industry estimates put man-made-fibre apparel at about 25 per cent of Bangladesh’s garment export revenues, compared with around 70 per cent of global clothing consumption. Polyester demand in Bangladesh is estimated to be growing by about 10 per cent a year. The Business Standard reported in September that annual local demand is around 140,000–160,000 tonnes for polyester staple fibre, while demand for polyester yarn is estimated at 500,000–550,000 tonnes. The same report said Modern Syntex already produces polyester staple fibre, filament yarn and PET chips, and meets nearly 21% of the country’s demand for polyester products. It also reported that a significant share of domestic demand is still met through imports. The ADB-backed expansion is therefore part of a broader effort to build domestic capacity, rather than Bangladesh’s first move into polyester production. summary: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16-18, the award recognised Naeimirad’s PolyBioDeg research into how the structure and properties of […] The post Paul Schlack Prize for Senbis bioplastics researcher appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16-18, the award recognised Naeimirad’s PolyBioDeg research into how the structure and properties of melt-spun bioplastic fibres influence both their mechanical performance during use and their subsequent biodegradation. Naeimirad is affiliated with Senbis and the University of Amsterdam. The Paul Schlack Prize is one of the fibre industry’s longest-established awards for young researchers. First awarded in 1971 and named after Paul Schlack, the inventor of polyamide 6, it is intended to encourage research and development in the manufacture, processing and application of man-made fibres in Europe. The €3,000 prize is awarded annually at Dornbirn following assessment by an independent jury. Naeimirad’s work addresses an increasingly important challenge for biodegradable polymers – achieving the mechanical and processing performance required during a product’s useful life while ensuring that the material can subsequently biodegrade under appropriate environmental conditions. It is an issue closely related to the wider development programme of Senbis at its base in Emmen, the Netherlands. The company used Dornbirn’s Innovation Day and Forum to present its GreenPearls range of biodegradable compounds for fibre and filament production. The materials are being engineered specifically around individual fibre-forming processes, with the aim of overcoming some of the processing and performance limitations traditionally associated with biodegradable polymers. title: AMANN Group: Strengthening Its Indian Footprint with Manufacturing, Innovation and Sustainable Thread Solutions
title_ko: AMANN 그룹: 제조, 혁신 및 지속 가능한 실 솔루션을 통해 인도 입지 강화
summary: With its state-of-the-art manufacturing facility in Ranipet now fully operational, AMANN Group is moving into a new phase of growth in India—combining global thread expertise with local manufacturing, faster delivery,… The post AMANN Group: Strengthening Its Indian Footprint with Manufacturing, Innovation and Sustainable Thread Solutions appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: With its state-of-the-art manufacturing facility in Ranipet now fully operational, AMANN Group is moving into a new phase of growth in India—combining global thread expertise with local manufacturing, faster delivery, application support and a growing portfolio of sustainable and high-performance solutions. Sanjeev Grewal, Regional Business Director – Asia, Middle East & Pacific , Amann Group For AMANN Group, India is no longer simply another market in its global network. It is emerging as a strategically important manufacturing and consumption centre, with opportunities extending across apparel, home textiles, footwear, leather and technical applications. The German thread specialist, which began its Indian journey with a trading operation in Chennai in 2007, has now taken a significant step forward by establishing a modern manufacturing facility at Ranipet in Tamil Nadu. The transformation reflects AMANN’s confidence in the long-term potential of the Indian textile and allied industries. After spending years understanding the market, its customers and their requirements, the company commenced construction of the Ranipet plant in 2022. Commercial production began towards the end of 2024, following a two-year delay caused by the pandemic. The facility has since completed its ramp-up phase and is now fully equipped to serve the Indian market with AMANN’s portfolio of products. For Sanjeev Grewal, Regional Business Director – Asia, Middle East & Pacific, the manufacturing investment represents much more than localisation. It is a clear expression of AMANN’s long-term commitment to India. From Trading to Manufacturing AMANN’s Indian journey began with a trading company in Chennai. content: A robotic hand developed by Chinese firm Agilink has been taught foundational Suzhou embroidery techniques by master craftswoman Fu Xianghong, including separating silk threads, threading a needle, stretching fabric on an embroidery hoop and stitching. The demonstration puts a robotic hand to work with one of the most delicate and deformable materials it can encounter. A silk thread can bend, slip and change shape with slight changes in contact. Splitting silk requires one finger to separate individual strands while others maintain support and tension. Twisting thread meanwhile requires opposing fingertips to maintain contact while allowing the thread to turn. Threading a needle and stitching add further demands on positioning, force and coordination. The OmniHand 3 Ultra combines 21 active degrees of freedom with a fully direct-drive architecture and tactile sensing across the fingertips, finger pads and palm. Vision-based tactile sensors at each fingertip detect changes in the contact surface, providing feedback as the hand handles thin, deformable materials. “A single silk thread gives OmniHand 3 Ultra’s fingertip dexterity a visible measure,” said Qiao Tianjie, vice president of Agibot and CEO of Agilink. “It also reveals the possibility of handing more delicate work to machines.” The demonstration comes as Agilink reaches a new stage of commercial scale. Spun out from Agibot in January 2026, the company has shipped more than 15,000 dexterous hands to date. In August, its OmniHand series competed across all eight dexterous-hand events at the World Humanoid Robot Games, winning seven gold, four silver and three bronze medals. title: Urmi Group puts drivers' children's drawings on trucks to promote road safety
summary: Urmi Group has launched an initiative to make its drivers more careful on the road, placing drawings and short messages from drivers' children on the back of its goods-carrying vehicles. Garment facto...
content: Urmi Group has launched an initiative to make its drivers more careful on the road, placing drawings and short messages from drivers' children on the back of its goods-carrying vehicles. Garment factories and other industrial units use thousands of trucks, covered vans and pickups every day to move goods. According to 2023 data from the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA), 1,389 trucks and covered vans and 370 pickups were among the 7,837 vehicles involved in road accidents, nearly 22 percent of the total. On Urmi Group's vehicles, each drawing carries one message: the father should drive carefully and return home safe at the end of the day. Some pictures show family stories, others a child's love for their father. The initiative draws on the "Children's Museum Project" of Japanese transport company Miyata Unyu. After a fatal road accident, the company began displaying drivers' children's drawings on its trucks. It reported that accidents fell by around 40 percent after drawings were added to 87 vehicles over six years. In 2019, the project became an independent organization and spread to many companies across Japan. In Bangladesh, painting pictures, slogans and artwork on the back of trucks is a long-standing tradition. Urmi Group is using this familiar space to build an emotional bond between drivers and their families. The group also believes the drawings will carry a humane message to pedestrians and other drivers. Urmi Group Managing Director Asif Ashraf said he experienced the idea first-hand while attending a seminar in Japan, and it moved him personally. "A child's drawing constantly reminds a driver that a family is waiting for him to return home safely," he said. content: As the global textile machinery industry prepares to meet at ITMA ASIA in Shanghai this November, Swedish textile technology companies are responding to a rapidly changing market with investment, innovation and new solutions. Growing competition from Asia, geopolitical uncertainty, new regulations and the accelerating impact of AI and digitalisation are reshaping the industry. Against this backdrop, TMAS members have had a busy 2026, with new facilities, product launches and technologies addressing automation, productivity, recycling and more resource-efficient textile manufacturing. Following a record 2025 and a number of bolt-on acquisitions, ACG Kinna has inaugurated a 1,000-square-metre expansion at its headquarters in Skene in response to growing demand for its complete textile and finished product line automation services. Imogo, a pioneer in industrial spray dyeing, has opened a new showroom, test centre and production hub in Kinnahult. Imogo introduced its first Dye-Max prototype in 2019 and completed its first industrial-scale installation in 2021. The new facility now enables brands and manufacturers to move from laboratory development to validated commercial production in one location. The centre features Imogo’s patented spray application technology, combining the Mini-Max laboratory system with a fully operational industrial-scale Dye-Max line for fabrics up to 2.4 metres wide and a production capacity of approximately 3 tons per day. Using as little as 0.7 litres of dye liquor per kilogram of fabric, Dye-Max delivers major reductions in water, energy, chemicals and wastewater compared with conventional dyeing. The training programme was organised under the initiative of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA), providing the participating students with […] The post NITER Students Gain Textile Technology and Industrial Exposure Through China Training Programme appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: Eight students from the National Institute of Textile Engineering and Research (NITER) have successfully completed an international training programme in China, gaining practical exposure to advanced textile technologies, industrial operations, academic practices and cultural heritage. The training programme was organised under the initiative of the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA), providing the participating students with an opportunity to experience China’s advanced textile manufacturing ecosystem beyond classroom-based learning. During the programme, the students explored modern textile production systems, automation, quality control and industrial management practices. Their exposure covered several key areas of textile manufacturing, including spinning technology, woven fabric dyeing, man-made fibre dyeing, fabric structure and textile design. As part of the industrial visits, the students visited Shengshan Group (至山集团), where they observed modern woven fabric dyeing operations and industrial production processes. They also gained insights into the integrated technologies and production capabilities used in China’s advanced spinning sector. The programme also included academic and cultural sessions at Zhejiang Agriculture and Business College. The students participated in sessions covering Chinese 3D media, tea culture and tea processing, Chinese language, traditional armour culture, and artificial intelligence-driven vehicle technology. At Shaoxing Secondary Technical School, the students received hands-on exposure to traditional natural indigo dyeing and printing techniques. content: Author: Ahmed Javed Jamal, Country Manager, Silkflex Bangladesh Limited How a screen-printing unit uses energy, how low-cure chemicals help, which savings are evidence-backed , and what to do first. Bangladesh has 883 textile printing units, and in most of them the largest energy user is the conveyor dryer or tunnel oven at the end of the line. Many of those units also deal with unreliable power, so every kilowatt-hour and every cubic meter of gas counts. Photo: Ahmed Javed Jamal, Country Manager, Silkflex Bangladesh Limited Published energy data for screen printing alone is thin, because most Bangladeshi studies cover the garment and textile sector as a whole. title: Denim Deal, United Repair Centre partner to scale circular denim
summary: Denim Deal has partnered with United Repair Centre (URC) to make garment repair a larger part of circular denim strategies. The partnership gives Denim Deal members access to URC’s European repair net...
content: Denim Deal has partnered with United Repair Centre (URC) to make garment repair a larger part of circular denim strategies. The partnership gives Denim Deal members access to URC’s European repair network and a member discount. Figure: Denim Deal aims to produce 1 billion pairs of jeans containing at least 20% post-consumer recycled cotton by 2030. The collaboration connects recycled cotton with longer garment life, two critical elements of denim circularity. Denim Deal aims to produce 1 billion pairs of jeans containing at least 20% post-consumer recycled cotton by 2030. The initiative also focuses on transparency, durability and circular production across major global regions. URC brings an established repair network to the partnership. Since launching in Amsterdam in 2022, it has completed more than 100,000 repairs for over 35 brands. Its workforce includes 50+ repair technicians across Amsterdam, London and Paris. Its brand partners include Patagonia, The North Face, Arc’teryx, Lululemon, Levi’s and Decathlon.Laura Vicaria, Program Director at Denim Deal, said durability connects material choice, design, repair and future recycling. The economic potential is also significant. A Circular Fashion Federation study found that Europe’s first-hand apparel “reinvent” segment could reach €71 billion, or about $80.9 billion, by 2030. Keeping jeans in use longer through durable design and professional repair can create another value pathway before recycling.

The final results were presented on 22 and 23 September at the ECOSYSTEX Conference in […] The post CISUTAC helps advance textile circularity appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: The CISUTAC project has concluded after four years of work across the European textile value chain, releasing a package of technologies, open data, consumer research and policy recommendations designed to support the transition towards a circular textile and clothing sector. The final results were presented on 22 and 23 September at the ECOSYSTEX Conference in Antwerp, where project partners outlined progress in repair, disassembly, recycling, consumer behaviour and policy development. CISUTAC tested new repair, disassembly and recycling technologies under real operating conditions. These included methods to significantly reduce the time needed for full zipper repairs, automated disassembly systems for difficult-to-recycle protective equipment and trials showing that recycled fibres can be spun into yarns with sufficient strength for use in new garments. The project has also produced open tools and datasets intended to make textile sorting faster and more consistent. Alongside the technical work, CISUTAC carried out large-scale consumer research supported by national awareness campaigns and local guidelines. The aim was to identify the factors influencing decisions to repair, reuse and purchase second-hand textiles, while exploring ways of encouraging more circular consumption habits. Policy work formed the third major strand of the project. Assessments of possible future scenarios for the European textile sector were used to develop recommendations covering waste management, public procurement, ecodesign, standardisation and Extended Producer Responsibility. summary: Primark has signed a multi-year offtake agreement with US textile recycler Circ for recycled polyester produced from textile waste, with the material expected to enter the retailer’s clothing ranges from 2029. The agreement is Primark’s first long-term offtake commitment with a textile-to-textile recycler and is intended to support Circ as it moves its polycotton recycling […] The post Primark signs long-term deal for Circ recycled polyester appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: Primark has signed a multi-year offtake agreement with US textile recycler Circ for recycled polyester produced from textile waste, with the material expected to enter the retailer’s clothing ranges from 2029. The agreement is Primark’s first long-term offtake commitment with a textile-to-textile recycler and is intended to support Circ as it moves its polycotton recycling technology to industrial scale. Circ, headquartered in Danville, Virginia, is currently developing its first industrial-scale recycling facility in France. The plant will process textile feedstock sourced internationally, including post-consumer and post-industrial waste from Europe, and will supply the recycled polyester covered by the Primark agreement. The volumes involved and financial terms of the agreement have not been disclosed. Circ’s patented process addresses one of the persistent problems in textile recycling – separating the polyester and cellulosic components of blended polycotton fabrics so that both can be recovered as raw materials for new textiles. The company produces two main outputs, Circ Polyester and Circ Lyocell, and has already worked with fashion brands on applications for the materials. The Primark agreement, however, represents a longer-term commitment to future commercial volumes as Circ builds up its production capacity. Peter Majeranowski, CEO of Circ, said long-term commitments from major fashion retailers would be important in moving textile-to-textile recycling from demonstration and early commercial projects towards large-scale production. For Primark, the agreement forms part of efforts to increase its use of recycled fibres and reduce its dependence on virgin polyester. title: How Much Will Fashion Let AI Decide?
summary: Our data shows that fashion’s use of AI is outpacing its willingness to trust it with important choices. But technology vendors see a clear progression from assisting to automating decision-making, paired with a move away from traditional interfaces. What is fashion comfortable letting AI decide today, and how fast is that frontier likely to move? The post How Much Will Fashion Let AI Decide? appeared first on The Interline .
content: Hey, welcome back to The Interline Podcast. Right now, fashion has a laser focus on product outcomes, and for good reason. The headline research tells us that industry growth is slowing down, which means brands are competing with one another for relative rather than absolute advantage. If you listened to our recent Mailroom episode , you heard Hannah Crump from BoF Insights talk about the fact that, in a low-growth environment like the one we’re living in, you can grow your slice of the pie by subtracting it from somebody else’s, but the overall dish isn’t getting any bigger. That makes optimising per-product profitability and reducing product- and collection-level risk essential. The data also shows that consumers are way less aligned with brands than they have been in a while, and tend to make selections based on specific products instead. That makes subjective attributes like style and fit, again on an individual product or small-collection basis, matter a lot. It makes more calculated, objective criteria like pricing, value, market positioning and market counter-positioning matter arguably even more when fashion companies make the choices that bring products to market. None of these outcomes just happens. Each is the result of a set of nested decisions that cascade down from ‘This is what we want to make, given the market conditions we’ve been handed’ to the granular choices that influence how that thing gets made, how effectively it meets its objectives and how it delivers its outcomes. Each of those decisions is also, especially right now, a target for potential automation.
